items.prompt: Why does your body raise its own temperature when you catch an infection?

options.label: It burns away the skin where the microbe entered
options.feedback: A fever raises the temperature of the whole body gently; it does no burning to the skin at all.

options.label: It dries out the blood so microbes cannot move through it
options.feedback: Blood stays just as liquid during a fever; the rise in temperature does not dry anything out.

options.label: A higher temperature makes it harder for many microbes to multiply
options.feedback: Correct — many microbes reproduce best within a narrow temperature range that a fever pushes past.

options.label: It signals to other people nearby to stay away
options.feedback: A fever is felt from the inside and produces no outward sign that could act as a signal to anyone else.

items.ok_line: Turning up the heat to slow the invader down.
items.ko_line: Ask what a change in temperature does to a living microbe.
items.exp_title: Turning the heat against the invader
items.exp_text: Many microbes multiply fastest within a fairly narrow band of temperature, close to the body's normal warmth, because the chemical reactions that let them grow work best there. When the brain's temperature control shifts its setting upward during an infection, the whole body warms a few degrees above that comfortable band, and the microbe's own chemistry slows down along with its ability to multiply. Meanwhile the body's own defensive cells tend to work faster in that same warmth, so raising the temperature tips the balance in the body's favour.

items.prompt: Why do you often shiver right before a fever sets in?

options.label: The brain has raised its temperature setpoint, and shivering generates heat to reach it
options.feedback: Correct — shivering is muscle activity working to warm the body up to the new setpoint.

options.label: The infection cools the blood suddenly
options.feedback: An infection does not cool the blood; if anything the body is working to raise its temperature, not lower it.

options.label: Shivering is the body trying to shake the microbe loose
options.feedback: Shivering does nothing to dislodge a microbe; it is muscle movement generating heat, not a physical shake aimed at the invader.

options.label: The skin closes its pores and traps cold air inside
options.feedback: Skin has no pores that open and close air passages that way; shivering works through muscle contraction, not trapped air.

items.ok_line: Muscles working hard to catch up to a new setpoint.
items.ko_line: Think about what shivering physically does to your muscles.
items.exp_title: Racing to catch up with a new setpoint
items.exp_text: The part of the brain that controls body temperature acts like a thermostat, and during an infection it resets that target higher than usual. The moment it does, the body below suddenly feels too cold compared to the new target, even though nothing about the room has changed, and it responds the way it would to any chill: by making muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly. That rapid contraction is shivering, and the friction and effort it takes generates heat that pushes body temperature up toward the new, higher target.

items.prompt: What job does pain do for the body when you touch something too hot?

options.label: It cools the skin down directly
options.feedback: Pain itself carries no cooling effect; it is a signal, not a temperature change.

options.label: It kills the skin cells that were touched
options.feedback: Pain is a message sent by nerves, not a process that destroys cells on its own.

options.label: It numbs the area so you stop noticing the heat
options.feedback: Pain does the opposite of numbing — it is what makes the heat impossible to ignore.

options.label: It sends an urgent signal that makes you pull away before damage spreads
options.feedback: Correct — the speed and urgency of pain is what drives that fast, protective withdrawal.

items.ok_line: An urgent message built to get you moving.
items.ko_line: Think about what pain makes you do in the moment, not what it does to the skin.
items.exp_text: Nerve endings in the skin sense damaging heat and fire off a signal that travels to the spinal cord and back to the muscles of the arm almost immediately, triggering the hand to pull away before the brain has even finished registering what happened. That same signal also reaches the brain a fraction later as the sharp sensation you call pain, which is what makes you remember to avoid that hot surface afterwards. The urgency of the sensation is what makes it so hard to ignore, which is exactly the point.

items.prompt: Why does a bruised area of skin often stay painful to the touch for a while, even lightly?

options.label: The bruise blocks nerve signals from reaching the brain at all
options.feedback: If signals were blocked, the area would feel numb rather than more sensitive to touch.

options.label: Damaged tissue releases chemicals that make nearby nerves more sensitive
options.feedback: Correct — those chemicals lower the threshold needed to trigger a pain signal.

options.label: Blood pooling under the skin presses directly on the brain
options.feedback: Blood from a bruise stays local to the injured tissue; it has no way of reaching the brain.

options.label: The skin grows an extra layer of nerve endings within hours
options.feedback: New nerve endings take far longer than that to grow; the change in sensitivity comes from the existing nerves, not new ones.

items.ok_line: The same touch, but nerves primed to react to less of it.
items.ko_line: Ask what changes about the nerves themselves rather than what blocks or grows them.
items.exp_text: Cells damaged by a bruise release chemical signals into the surrounding tissue as part of the body's response to injury, and those same chemicals act on the nerve endings nearby, lowering the amount of pressure needed to set off a pain signal. A touch that would normally pass unnoticed is now enough to trigger one, because the nerves have effectively had their trigger turned down. That heightened sensitivity fades as the tissue repairs itself and those chemical signals clear away.

items.prompt: Why does the skin around a scraped knee swell up soon after the injury?

options.label: Blood vessels there become leakier, letting fluid seep into the tissue
options.feedback: Correct — that extra fluid collecting in the tissue is what causes the swelling.

options.label: The wound fills with air trapped under the skin
options.feedback: There is no mechanism by which a scrape traps air under the skin; the swelling is fluid, not air.

options.label: New skin cells are already piling up at the site
options.feedback: New skin cells take longer to form; the early swelling happens before much rebuilding has begun.

options.label: The muscles beneath tighten and push outward
options.feedback: Muscle tightening plays no part in this kind of swelling, which happens right at the skin's surface.

items.ok_line: Fluid seeping out is what makes the area puff up.
items.ko_line: Ask what is filling the swollen space, not what is pushing on it from below.
items.exp_text: Chemical signals released by damaged tissue make the walls of small blood vessels near the injury more porous than usual, so fluid that would normally stay inside the vessel leaks out into the surrounding tissue instead. That extra fluid has nowhere to drain quickly, so it collects around the wound and pushes the tissue outward, which is what you see as swelling. The same leaky vessels also let more defensive cells slip out of the blood and into the injured tissue, so the swelling arrives alongside help rather than instead of it.

items.prompt: Why does a fever that stays too high for too long become dangerous rather than helpful?

options.label: It becomes helpful again once it passes a high enough point
options.feedback: Fever does not become safer the higher it climbs; the risk only grows as heat pushes further past what the body can tolerate.

options.label: It confuses the microbe into multiplying faster
options.feedback: Heat slows most microbes down rather than speeding them up; an extreme fever does not reverse that effect.

options.label: Extreme heat starts to damage the body's own proteins along with the microbe's
options.feedback: Correct — past a certain point, heat harms the body's own cells too, not just the invader.

options.label: It stops the heart from pumping blood at all
options.feedback: A dangerously high fever puts real strain on the body, but it does not simply stop the heart from working.

items.ok_line: The same heat that slows the invader can start to harm its host too.
items.ko_line: Think about what heat does to any protein, including the body's own.
items.exp_title: A weapon that can turn on its owner
items.exp_text: The proteins that make up the body's own cells rely on holding a particular folded shape to work properly, and enough heat can shake that shape apart the same way it can damage a microbe's proteins. A fever that stays within the usual protective range mostly troubles the invader, whose proteins tend to be more easily disrupted than the body's own. Push the temperature high enough for long enough, though, and the body's own proteins start to lose their shape too, which is when a fever stops helping and starts to cause harm.

items.prompt: Why does an inflamed joint, such as a sprained ankle, feel stiff and harder to move?

options.label: The bones inside the joint temporarily fuse together
options.feedback: Bones do not fuse from a sprain; the joint's own structure stays the same, only the surrounding tissue changes.

options.label: Swelling in the tissue around the joint restricts how far it can bend
options.feedback: Correct — the extra fluid crowding the area physically limits the joint's range of motion.

options.label: The muscles around it lose their ability to contract
options.feedback: The muscles can still contract; what limits movement is crowding around the joint, not a loss of muscle function.

options.label: Pain signals shut down the nerves controlling the joint
options.feedback: Nerves keep working during a sprain; pain makes movement unpleasant rather than shutting the nerves down.

items.ok_line: Less room to move, because fluid has crowded the space.
items.ko_line: Ask what physically takes up extra space around the joint.
items.exp_title: Crowded space, less room to bend
items.exp_text: A sprain stretches or tears the tissue holding a joint together, and the injury triggers the same response as any damaged tissue: blood vessels nearby become leakier and fluid pools in the space around the joint. That extra fluid crowds the same tight space the joint needs in order to bend and straighten, so the range of movement shrinks simply because there is less room to move through. The stiffness eases as the swelling goes down and that space opens back up.

items.prompt: Why does pressing on a swollen, inflamed area usually hurt more than pressing on unaffected skin nearby?

options.label: Inflamed skin has lost its sense of touch entirely
options.feedback: If touch were lost, pressing would produce no extra sensation at all rather than more pain.

options.label: The swelling contains no nerve endings, so pain builds up unreleased
options.feedback: The nerve endings are still there and are exactly what is detecting the extra pressure; nothing about the swelling removes them.

options.label: Inflamed areas are always colder and more fragile
options.feedback: Inflamed tissue tends to run warmer rather than colder, and the added pain comes from pressure on stretched tissue, not fragility.

options.label: The tissue is already stretched tight by fluid, so added pressure strains it further
options.feedback: Correct — pressing on already-stretched tissue pushes it closer to the nerves' limit.

items.ok_line: Already stretched, and pressure stretches it a little further.
items.ko_line: Think about what fluid has already done to the tissue before you even touch it.
items.exp_text: Fluid gathering in inflamed tissue stretches it outward, and that stretching alone is already close to the point where the nerve endings inside start to fire. Pressing down adds further pressure on top of that existing stretch, pushing those same nerves past the point they can tolerate quietly, so the same amount of pressure feels far sharper there than on unaffected skin. That is also why an inflamed area often hurts even without being touched, since the stretching from the fluid is doing part of the work on its own.

items.prompt: Why does drinking more fluids help while you have a fever?

options.label: A higher body temperature makes you lose water faster through sweat and breathing
options.feedback: Correct — extra fluid replaces what a feverish body is losing more quickly than usual.

options.label: Extra fluid lowers your body's temperature setpoint directly
options.feedback: Drinking fluids does not reset the brain's temperature control; that setpoint changes for other reasons during illness.

options.label: Fluids carry oxygen straight to fighting cells
options.feedback: Oxygen is carried through the lungs and blood, not delivered by the fluids you drink.

options.label: Fluids wash the microbe straight out through the skin
options.feedback: Drinking fluids has no route to flush a microbe out through the skin; the body deals with the infection internally.

items.ok_line: Replacing what a warmer body is losing faster.
items.ko_line: Think about what a higher temperature does to how much water the body loses.
items.exp_text: A body running a fever sweats more and breathes a little faster than usual, both of which carry water out of the body along with the heat they release. If that lost water is not replaced, the blood becomes thicker and harder for the heart to circulate, which makes every other part of fighting the infection more difficult. Drinking enough fluid keeps that loss balanced, so the body can keep sweating to release heat without running short of water to do it with.

items.prompt: Why does resting more than usual often come naturally when you are fighting off an infection?

options.label: Resting stops the infection from spreading through the blood
options.feedback: Movement does not spread infection through the blood in this way; resting is about energy, not about containing spread.

options.label: Muscles stop working completely during an infection
options.feedback: Muscles still work during an infection; they simply have less spare energy available, rather than none at all.

options.label: Fighting an infection uses a large share of the body's energy, leaving less for activity
options.feedback: Correct — energy spent on defence is energy not available for moving around.

options.label: Lying down lowers body temperature back to normal
options.feedback: Position has little effect on body temperature; the fever continues whether you are lying down or standing.

items.ok_line: Energy spent defending is energy not spent moving.
items.ko_line: Think about where the body's energy is going while it fights an infection.
items.exp_text: Multiplying defensive cells, raising body temperature and repairing damaged tissue all draw heavily on the same store of energy that would otherwise power movement and alertness. As that energy gets redirected toward fighting the infection, less is left over for the muscles and the mind, which is felt as tiredness and a pull toward lying still. Resting also means less energy is spent on activity that is not helping the fight, leaving more of it available for the cells doing the actual work.
